title: Sweet scent of success

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Innovation and entrepreneurship, in the right mix, can bring spectacular results to a business. Creators tap into something which consumers cannot wait to use. Other successful innovators have rethought how a service is provided or the way business is done. However, most ideas never make it to the market. Grant Kearney, chief executive of the Innovation Xchange in Australia, which connects businesses to innovation networks, says he hears of great business ideas that he knows will never get on the market. ‘Ideas by themselves are absolutely useless,’ he says. ‘An idea only becomes innovation when it is connected to the right resources and capabilities.’

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: One of Australia’s latest innovation successes stems from a lemon-scented bathroom cleaner called ‘Shower Power’, the formula for which was concocted in a factory in Yatala, Queensland. In 1995, Tom Quinn and John Heron bought a struggling cleaning products business, OzKleen, for A$250,000. It was selling 100 different kinds of cleaning products, mainly in bulk. The business was not profitable, the cleaning formulas were ineffective and environmentally harsh, and there were few regular clients. However, by 2004, it was claimed that Shower Power had become the top-selling bathroom cleaning product in Australia. Over 12 months, almost four million bottles of OzKleen’s Shower Power products were sold. The company’s turnover reached A$11 million, with 70% of business being exports. In particular, Shower Power was making big inroads on the British market.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: OzKleen’s turnaround began when Quinn and Heron hired an industrial chemist to revitalise the product line. Market research showed that people were looking for a better cleaner for the bathroom, universally regarded as the hardest room in the home to clean. The company also wanted to make the product formulas more environmentally friendly. One of Tom Quinn’s sons, Peter, began working with the chemist on the formulas, looking at the potential for citrus-based cleaning products. He detested all the chlorine-based cleaning products that dominated the market. Peter Quinn looked at citrus ingredients, such as orange peel, to replace the petroleum by-products in cleaners. He is credited with finding the Shower Power formula. ‘The recipe is in a vault somewhere and in my head,’ he says. The company is the sole owner of the intellectual property.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: To begin with, Shower Power was sold only in commercial quantities, but Tom Quinn decided to sell it in 750ml bottles after it was so well received by customers at their retail store at Beenleigh, near Brisbane. Customers were travelling long distances to buy supplies. Other retail customers began writing to OzKleen to say how good Shower Power was. ‘We made a dummy label and went to see Woolworths (the supermarket chain),’ Tom Quinn says. The Woolworths buyer, who was responsible for buying products to sell at the supermarket, took a bottle home and was able to remove a stain from her basin that had been impossible to shift. From that point on, she championed the product and OzKleen had its first supermarket order, for a pallet of Shower Power worth A$3000. ‘We were delighted,’ says OzKleen’s financial controller, Belinda McDonnell.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Shower Power was released in Australian Woolworths supermarkets in 1997 and became the top-selling product in its category within six months. Everybody at the factory had to collaborate, labelling and bottling Shower Power to keep up with requirements. OzKleen stopped manufacturing all other products and rebuilt the business around Shower Power. ‘This stage,’ recalls McDonnell, ‘was very tough. Cashflow was very difficult,’ she says. OzKleen had to pay special fees to the supermarket chain for selling a ‘new’ product, which also squeezed profit margins.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: OzKleen’s next breakthrough came when the daughter of a Coles Myer executive used the product while on holiday in Queensland and convinced her father that Shower Power should be sold in Coles supermarkets. Despite the product’s success, Peter Quinn says the company was wary of how long the sales would last, and hesitated to spend money on upgrading the manufacturing process. As a result, he remembers long periods of working 24 hours per day to keep up with orders. Small tanks were still being used, so batches were small and bottles were labelled and filled manually. The privately owned OzKleen relied on cash flow to expand. ‘The equipment could not keep up with demand,’ Peter Quinn says. Eventually, a new bottling machine was bought for A$50,000 in the hope of streamlining production, but this didn’t work. Since then he has developed a new automated bottling machine that can control the amount of foam produced in the liquid, so that bottles can be filled more effectively. The machine was patented.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Peter Quinn says OzKleen spends as much money as they require on research and development and that can be considerable sums. ‘If I need it, I get it. It’s about doing something simple that no one else is doing. Most of these things are just sitting in front of people … it’s just seeing the opportunities.’ With a tried and tested product, OzKleen expanded overseas and developed more Power-brand household products. ‘We wanted to export as soon as we could because we realised we had the same opportunities worldwide.’ The Quinn and Heron families continue to be involved in managing the company. OzKleen has also been approached with offers to buy the company, but Tom Quinn says he is happy with things as they are.
